error.operatorNeedsExpr: The "{{op}}" operator must be preceded by an expression (position {{pos}}).

build.title: Automaton from the expression (lecture notes 3.20)
build.detail: The expression is built inside out, as 3.20 proves its language regular. A letter a gets a single a-transition, ε a single accepting state, ∅ a single state that never accepts (3.3). r₁ + r₂: a new start state with ε-transitions into both start states, accepting where either one does (3.4). r₁r₂: ε-transitions from the first one's accepting states into the second one's start, accepting where the second one does (3.9). r*: a new start state, accepting too, with an ε-transition into the old start and ε-transitions back from the accepting states (3.10). r? means r + ε. Result: {{count}} states — det(·) turns it into a DFA.

unparseableCell.title: Unparseable cell
unparseableCell.detail: A cell is either a YAML definition (with a Machine / Grammar key) or an expression, optionally named: "name = expression".

duplicateDefinition.title: Duplicate definition: "{{name}}"
duplicateDefinition.detail: The name is defined by both cell {{other}} and cell {{index}} — the first definition wins; remove or rename the others.

circularDependency.title: Circular dependency
circularDependency.detail: The definition of "{{name}}" (indirectly) refers to itself: {{chain}}. Break the cycle.

brokenDependency.title: Broken dependency: {{missing}}
brokenDependency.detail: The referenced cell is broken or can't be evaluated yet — fix that one first.

machine.startNotInStates: The start state ({{start}}) is not among the states
machine.acceptNotInStates: The accepting state ({{state}}) is not among the states

badStoragesField.title: The storages field expects key-value pairs
badStoragesField.detail:
For example:
  storages:
    v1: stack
    v2:
      type: queue
      charset: A, B
      init: A

badInputField.title: The input field ({{input}}) is not the id of a storage
badInputField.detail: Use "head" (the read head), or the name of one of the storages: {{storages}}.

noAcceptSuggestEmptyStorages.title: No accepting state — for acceptance by empty storages, use acceptMode: emptyStorages
noAcceptSuggestEmptyStorages.detail: Without an accepting state and in finalState mode, the machine recognizes the empty language.

invalidTransition.title: Invalid transition: "{{line}}"
invalidTransition.detail: This machine's transitions read {{shape}}: δ's arguments in parentheses, an arrow, then its value, every part written out (ε too).

machine.unknownToState: Unknown target state in the transition: "{{state}}"

noAcceptState.title: No accepting state
noAcceptState.detail: The machine therefore recognizes the empty language.

nondeterministicMachine.title: Nondeterministic machine: more than one transition can match in state {{state}}
nondeterministicMachine.detail: The simulation follows every branch; click a highlighted edge on the graph to pick a specific branch.

storageCharsetNotOneSymbol.title: “{{symbol}}” in the alphabet of {{storageId}} is not one symbol
storageCharsetNotOneSymbol.detail: List the alphabet's symbols one by one, separated by commas. A symbol with a subscript is written with _, like {{example}}.

blankNotInTapeCharset.title: The blank _ is missing from the alphabet of {{storageId}}
blankNotInTapeCharset.detail: A tape holds blanks wherever nothing is written, so the blank is one of its symbols: _ ∈ Γ.

blankInInput.title: The blank _ cannot be an input symbol
blankInInput.detail: The input is written onto the tape {{storageId}}, where _ marks the empty cells: _ ∈ Γ \ Σ.

inputNotInStorageCharset.title: The alphabet of {{storageId}} lacks the input symbols {{symbols}}
inputNotInStorageCharset.detail: The input is written onto this storage, so every input symbol is one of its symbols too: Σ ⊆ Γ.

initNotInStorageCharset.title: The initial content of {{storageId}} uses “{{symbol}}”, which is not in its alphabet

unknownStorageSymbol.title: Unknown symbol “{{symbol}}” for {{storageId}}
unknownStorageSymbol.detail: Line: "{{line}}". The alphabet of {{storageId}} is Γ = {{gamma}} — any other symbol it may hold goes in its charset.

fieldHints.variables: The variables, e.g. variables: S, A, B
fieldHints.init: The start variable, e.g. init: S
fieldHints.charset: The terminals, e.g. charset: a, b
fieldHints.rules: The rules, e.g. rules: [S -> aA | b]

grammar.startNotInNonterminals: The start variable ({{start}}) is not among the variables

overlappingSymbols.title: Conflicting symbols: {{symbols}}
overlappingSymbols.detail: A symbol cannot be both a terminal and a variable.

emptyAlternative.title: Empty alternative in the rule: "{{line}}"
emptyAlternative.detail: Write ε (or eps) for the empty word, e.g. "S -> aS | ε".

invalidRule.title: Invalid rule: "{{line}}"
invalidRule.detail: Form: LEFT -> RIGHT1 | RIGHT2 — e.g. "S -> aA | b". Write ε (or eps) for the empty word.

grammar.unknownSymbolLeft: Unknown symbol on the left side of the rule: "{{symbol}}"
grammar.ruleDetail: Rule: "{{line}}". Every symbol must be listed in charset or variables.

leftMissingNonterminal.title: The left side of the rule contains no variable: "{{line}}"
leftMissingNonterminal.detail: In a generative grammar, the left side must contain at least one variable.

grammar.unknownSymbolRight: Unknown symbol on the right side of the rule: "{{symbol}}"

terminalNotOneChar.title: The terminal “{{symbol}}” is longer than one character
terminalNotOneChar.detail: Terminals are the characters of the words, so each is a single character. Variables may have subscripts: X_a, C_1.

ambiguousSubscript.title: “{{text}}” is ambiguous
ambiguousSubscript.detail: It could be the variable {{name}} or the symbols {{separate}}. Write {{name}} with _ for the variable, or separate the symbols with a space. ({{line}})

rangeTooLarge.title: Range too large in the {{field}} field: "{{range}}"

unknownStorageType.title: Unknown storage type for the "{{id}}" storage
unknownStorageType.detail:
Allowed: stack, queue, tape — with an alphabet and an initial content:
  v1:
    type: stack
    charset: Z, A
    init: Z

unknownMove.title: Unknown move: "{{tokens}}" ({{storageId}})
unknownMove.detail: Line: "{{line}}". Allowed: R (right), L (left), S (stay) — the YAML always uses these English letters, whatever the interface's language.

oneSymbol.title: “{{tokens}}” is more than one symbol ({{storageId}})
oneSymbol.detail: An operation takes a single symbol off the storage (or ε for nothing). A symbol with a subscript is written with _, like {{example}}. ({{line}})

tapeOneSymbol.title: “{{tokens}}” is not one tape symbol ({{storageId}})
tapeOneSymbol.detail: Line: "{{line}}". A tape cell always holds exactly one symbol — an empty one the blank _.

badName.title: “{{name}}” is not a name
badName.detail: A name is a single letter with an optional subscript — for example {{suggestion}}. Type _ to start the subscript; digits right after the letter go there by themselves (M1 is M₁).

infiniteOnlyForTape.title: Storage "{{id}}": infinite only applies to a tape
infiniteOnlyForTape.detail: A stack or a queue has no extent to choose — leave the infinite key out.

badInfinite.title: Storage "{{id}}": unknown tape extent "{{value}}"
badInfinite.detail: infinite: right — a tape infinite to the right from its first cell, as in the lecture notes (the default); infinite: both — a tape infinite in both directions.

writableOnlyForTape.title: Storage "{{id}}": writable only applies to a tape
writableOnlyForTape.detail: A stack or a queue is always written — leave the writable key out.

badWritable.title: Storage "{{id}}": writable is true or false, not "{{value}}"
badWritable.detail: writable: true — the machine may write on the tape too; writable: false — it only reads it. By default the input tape of a machine with several storages is read-only, as on the k-tape Turing machine of the lecture notes (9.9); every other tape is writable.

needsDeterministic.title: The {{op}} operation requires a deterministic automaton
needsDeterministic.detail: Nondeterminism found: {{spots}}{{ellipsis}}. In a deterministic automaton every (state, symbol) pair has exactly one successor state and there is no ε-transition. The subset construction (determinization, lecture notes 2.16) builds an equivalent DFA, ε-transitions included.

needsComplete.title: The {{op}} operation requires a complete automaton
needsComplete.detail: Missing transitions: {{spots}}{{ellipsis}} — {{count}} (state, symbol) pairs have no transition defined in total. To complete it, we introduce a new "trap" (rejecting) state and route every missing transition there.

alreadyFree.title: The automaton is already ε-free
alreadyFree.detail: There is no ε-transition, so the operation returns the automaton unchanged.

step1.title: 1. Computing ε-closures
step1.detail: For every state q: E(q) = the set of states reachable from q using only ε-transitions (including q itself).

step2.title: 2. Introducing new transitions
step2.detail: δ'(q, a) = E(δ(E(q), a)) — transitions reachable through the ε-closure are made direct.

step3.title: 3. Extending the accepting states
step3.detailChanged: If E(q) contains an accepting state, q becomes accepting too. New accepting states: {{list}}.
step3.detailUnchanged: No state's ε-closure contains a new accepting state, so the accepting set is unchanged.

alreadyDeterministic.title: The automaton is already deterministic
alreadyDeterministic.detail: Every (state, symbol) pair has at most one transition and there is no ε-transition — the subset construction only creates the reachable one-element sets (and ∅ where a transition is missing).

step.title: Subset construction (lecture notes 2.16)
step.detail: The new states are sets of the old ones; the start state is {{start}}. For every set R reached and every letter a: δ'(R, a) = ⋃ δ(r, a) over r ∈ R — where R has several elements, the parts are shown one by one. Only the sets reachable from the start are built, and a set accepts if it contains an accepting state.
step.detailEpsilon: The new states are sets of the old ones; the start state is {{startExpr}} = {{start}}. For every set R reached and every letter a: δ'(R, a) = ⋃ E(δ(r, a)) over r ∈ R — a letter is read, then any ε-transitions may follow. Where R has several elements, the parts E(δ(r, a)) are shown one by one. Only the sets reachable from the start are built, and a set accepts if it contains an accepting state.

result.title: Result
result.detail: {{count}} states were produced out of the possible 2^{{exponent}} = {{possible}} subsets. Accepting: {{accept}}.

closures.title: ε-closures (lecture notes 2.16)
closures.detail: E(q) is the set of states reachable from q along ε-transitions — any number of them —, q included. The new automaton works with these closures: its start state is the closure of the start state, and after a letter it takes the closure of where the letter leads.

emptySet.title: The empty set ∅ appears — a trap state
emptySet.detail: Where a letter leads nowhere, δ'(R, a) = ∅: the empty set is a state too — it never accepts, and every letter keeps it there. So the result is a complete DFA.

alreadyComplete.title: The automaton is already complete
alreadyComplete.detail: Every (state, symbol) pair has a transition — nothing to do.

nameTaken.title: The state name "{{trap}}" already exists
nameTaken.detail: Completion needs a new, not-yet-used trap-state name.

step.title: Introducing the trap state: {{trap}} (lecture notes 2.10)
step.detail: The new state {{trap}} is not accepting, and every symbol maps it to itself — once there, it can no longer accept. The missing transitions are routed here.

allReachable.title: Every state is reachable
allReachable.detail: Every state is reachable from the start state — there is nothing to drop.

step.title: Removing unreachable states
step.detail: The states reachable from the start state by a breadth-first traversal remain. Removed: {{removed}}.

unreachableStates.title: Unreachable states
unreachableStates.detail: No word leads from the start state into {{states}}. The notes (2.29) leave such states out of the finished automaton; here they go first, which gives the same result.

step1.title: Initial partition: 0-equivalence (lecture notes 2.4.1)
step1.detail: A₁ = Q − F and A₂ = F: the empty word already tells the non-accepting and the accepting states apart. {{partition}}

refine.title: Round {{round}}: {{round}}-equivalence
refine.detail: Two states stay together when every letter takes them into the same group. Splitting: {{splits}}. New partition: {{partition}}. Now the states no word of length at most {{round}} tells apart are together ({{round}}-equivalence, 2.27).

fixpoint.title: Round {{round}}: nothing splits
fixpoint.detail: In every group, every letter takes all states into the same group: {{round}}-equivalence is the same as {{prev}}-equivalence, and then no longer word tells the states apart either (2.27). The groups are the equivalence classes: {{partition}}.

alreadyMinimal.title: The automaton was already minimal
alreadyMinimal.detail: Every state ended up in its own equivalence class.

minimized.title: Minimized: {{before}} → {{after}} states
minimized.detail: States grouped into the same class are linguistically indistinguishable: they accept/reject every word the same way.

build.title: The new automaton from the classes (lecture notes 2.29)
build.detail: Every class is a state. A letter takes all states of a class into the same class — that is the transition. The start state is the class of the old one, {{start}}; the accepting states are the classes of accepting states: {{accept}}.

whyDfa.title: Why is a DFA required?
whyDfa.detail: For an NFA, flipping the accepting states does NOT yield the complement language: an NFA accepts a word if an accepting path EXISTS — after flipping, a rejecting path may still exist and become accepting too.

whyComplete.title: Why is completeness required?
whyComplete.detail: If a transition is missing somewhere, the automaton gets "stuck" and rejects. The complement should accept these words instead — this requires completing the automaton with a trap state first.

step.title: Flipping the accepting states (lecture notes 3.6)
step.detail: In a complete DFA, every word runs along exactly one path, so swapping accepting/rejecting states yields exactly the complement language. New accepting set: {{accept}}.

hasEpsilon.title: The {{part}} automaton contains an ε-transition
hasEpsilon.detail: The product construction (running both in parallel) expects deterministic, complete automata, because the two automata must step in sync, symbol by symbol. An ε-transition would break this.

nondeterministic.title: The {{part}} automaton is nondeterministic
nondeterministic.detail: The states of the product automaton are (p, q) pairs, with δ((p,q),a) = (δ₁(p,a), δ₂(q,a)) — this requires both δ's to be single-valued.

incomplete.title: The {{part}} automaton is not complete
incomplete.detailUnion: If one automaton gets stuck, the pair can no longer step even though the other could still run — for a union, the other automaton's acceptance still matters. Completion (a trap state) fixes this.
incomplete.detailOther: If one automaton gets stuck, the pair can no longer step even though the other could still run — the result would be incorrect. Completion (a trap state) fixes this.

acceptRule.union: (p,q) is accepting if p OR q is accepting
acceptRule.intersect: (p,q) is accepting if p AND q are both accepting
acceptRule.difference: (p,q) is accepting if p is accepting but q is NOT (L₁ \ L₂)

step.title: Product construction ({{mode}}, lecture notes 3.4)
step.detail: The two automata are run in parallel: the states are (p,q) pairs, δ((p,q),a) = (δ₁(p,a), δ₂(q,a)). Acceptance: {{acceptRule}}. Only reachable pairs are built.

extend.title: The {{part}} automaton over the common alphabet (lecture notes 3.4)
extend.detail: {{name}} has no transition on {{missing}}: over Σ = {{sigma}} it is an incomplete automaton, so it is completed first (2.10) — every missing transition leads into a new trap state {{trap}}, which never leaves. Its language does not change.

info.title: Union built via ε-construction
info.detail: An ε-transition leads from a new start state into both automata's start states. The result is an ε-NFA — det(·) turns it into a DFA. (A union of complete DFAs can also be done with the product construction.)

step.title: Union with ε-transitions (lecture notes 3.4)
step.detail: New start state {{start}}, ε-transitions: {{start}} → {{m1start}}, {{start}} → {{bstart}}. Accepting states: the union of both automata's accepting states.

step.title: Concatenation (lecture notes 3.9)
step.detail: An ε-transition leads from every accepting state of the first automaton to the second automaton's start state ({{start}}). Accepting: only the second automaton's accepting states. The result is an ε-NFA.

step.title: Kleene closure (star, lecture notes 3.10)
step.detail: New start state {{start}} (also accepting — so the empty word is in the language too), an ε-transition to the original start state, and from every accepting state an ε-transition back to {{start}} for repetition.

step.title: Reversal (lecture notes 4.23)
step.detail: Every transition's direction is reversed, an ε-transition leads from the new start state ({{start}}) to the original accepting states, and the original start state becomes the sole accepting state. L(Mᴿ) = { wᴿ : w ∈ L(M) }.

numbering.title: Numbering the states (lecture notes 3.21)
numbering.detail: The states are numbered 1…{{n}}; the start state {{start}} gets 1. r(p, q, t) describes the words that lead from state p to state q while every intermediate state is among 1…t.

base.title: r(p, q, 0) — no intermediate state
base.detail: The letters on the p → q edges, plus ε when p = q (and for an ε-edge); ∅ when there is nothing.

round.title: r(p, q, {{t}}) — passing through state {{state}} is allowed too
round.detail: r(p, q, {{t}}) = r(p, q, {{prev}}) + r(p, {{t}}, {{prev}}) r({{t}}, {{t}}, {{prev}})* r({{t}}, q, {{prev}}) — the word either avoids state {{t}}, or reaches it, returns to it any number of times and then leaves for q. Simplified with identities such as ∅ + r = r, r∅ = ∅, (a + ε)* = a*, (a + ε)a* = a* and b + a*b = a*b.

result.title: Result
result.detail: The language is the union of r(1, q, {{n}}) over the accepting states q: {{terms}} = {{regex}}
result.detailNone: There is no accepting state, so the language is empty: ∅.

tooLarge.title: The regular expression grows too large
tooLarge.detail: At step t = {{t}} (of {{n}}) an expression grew longer than {{limit}} characters. Minimize the automaton first — toRegex(min(…)) — for a much shorter expression.

multiCharSymbol.title: The symbol “{{symbol}}” is longer than one character
multiCharSymbol.detail: In a regular expression every letter is a single character, so every symbol of the alphabet must be one character long.

step.title: Renaming the states
step.detail: States get the names A, B, C… in the order they're visited starting from the start state. The language does not change.

counterexampleSearch.title: Searching for a counterexample in the product automaton
counterexampleSearch.detail: The two automata (made complete and deterministic) are run in parallel, searching for the shortest word accepted by exactly one of them. Found: "{{word}}".

proof.title: Proving equivalence
proof.detail: In every reachable (p,q) state pair of the product automaton, p and q's acceptance status agree, so there is no distinguishing word — the two automata recognize the same language.

det.title: Determinizing {{name}} (lecture notes 2.16)
det.detail: {{name}} is not a complete deterministic automaton, so the subset construction turns it into a complete DFA: {{count}} states.

extend.title: {{name}} over the common alphabet (lecture notes 2.10)
extend.detail: {{name}} has no transition on {{missing}}: those letters lead into a new trap state {{trap}}, so the alphabet is common and the language stays the same.

search.title: Looking for a distinguishing word in the product automaton (lecture notes 5.3)
search.detailFound: L({{a}}) = L({{b}}) exactly when (L({{a}}) ∩ ¬L({{b}})) ∪ (¬L({{a}}) ∩ L({{b}})) = ∅ (5.3). The two automata run side by side (the product automaton, 3.4), and a breadth-first search looks for the first reachable pair (p, q) where exactly one accepts. The table shows the pairs in the order of the search, up to the one found.
search.detailNone: L({{a}}) = L({{b}}) exactly when (L({{a}}) ∩ ¬L({{b}})) ∪ (¬L({{a}}) ∩ L({{b}})) = ∅ (5.3). The two automata run side by side (the product automaton, 3.4): in all {{count}} reachable pairs (p, q) both accept or both reject, so the language of the difference is empty.

needsContextFree.title: This operation ({{op}}) needs rules of the form A → α
needsContextFree.detail: Every rule's left-hand side must be a single variable (lecture notes 6.3.1) — ε-rules are fine. The Chomsky classification panel shows which rule breaks this.

classify.startEpsilonNotAllowed: {{start}} → ε is only allowed if {{start}} occurs on no right-hand side — but it does here
classify.deletingRule: {{rule}} is an ε-rule (ε is only allowed as S → ε)
classify.epsilonNotOnStart: {{rule}} — an ε-rule not on the start variable
classify.startOnRightWithEpsilon: alongside {{start}} → ε, {{start}} also occurs on a right-hand side — so the grammar is not in ε-free form
classify.notRegularRule: rule {{rule}} is not of the form A → aB or A → a
classify.leftNotSingleVariable: the left side of rule {{rule}} is not a single variable
classify.notContextSensitive: rule {{rule}} is not of the form βAγ → βαγ (a variable A replaced in place by a nonempty α)

needsRightLinear.title: Only a right-linear grammar can be turned into a finite automaton
needsRightLinear.detail: Every rule must be A → aB or A → a (type 3), or more generally A → uB, A → u, A → B or A → ε with a terminal word u. The construction (lecture notes 4.20): every variable becomes a state; A → aB becomes the transition A →a B; A → a a transition into a new accepting state E; A → ε makes A accepting.

step.title: Right-linear grammar → NFA (lecture notes 4.20)
step.detail: Every variable becomes a state, the start variable is the start state, and a new state {{end}} is the accepting one. From A → aB: an a-transition from A to B; from A → a: an a-transition into {{end}}; with S → ε, S accepts too. A longer word u in A → uB or A → u gets new states in between, A → B becomes an ε-transition and A → ε makes A accepting.

renamed.title: Some states got A_q variable names

step.title: Variables for the states (lecture notes 4.20)
step.detail: Every state q gets a variable A_q — the state's own name when it already is a valid variable name. The start state's variable is the start variable.

needsEpsilonFree.title: An automaton without ε-transitions is needed for a grammar
needsEpsilonFree.detail: The construction of lecture notes 4.20 turns a transition δ(q, a) = p into A_q → aA_p — an ε-transition ({{list}}) would give a rule A_q → A_p, which no type-3 grammar has. Remove the ε-transitions first.

newStart.title: A start state with no incoming transition (lecture notes 4.19)
newStart.detail: {{start}} accepts, so the grammar gets S → ε — and then S may occur on no right-hand side. But transitions lead into {{start}}: a new state {{copy}}, a copy of {{start}} (accepting as well), takes them over and moves on just as {{start}} does. The language stays the same.

rules.title: Rules from the transitions
rules.detail: δ(q, a) = p gives A_q → aA_p: after reading a, the derivation goes on from p. When p accepts, A_q → a as well: the word may end there. When the start state accepts, S → ε. Every rule is A → aB or A → a, and S → ε comes only with S on no right-hand side: the grammar is type 3 and generates the automaton's language.

needsContextFree.title: Only a grammar of A → α rules can be turned into a pushdown automaton
needsContextFree.detail: In the construction (lecture notes 7.12) the stack holds the rest of the sentential form, and a variable on its top is replaced by a right-hand side — so every left-hand side must be a single variable. The Chomsky classification panel shows which rule breaks this.

emptyStackInfo.title: Built a PDA that accepts by empty stack
emptyStackInfo.detail: The stack holds the derivation's current sentential form. If a variable is on top of the stack, a rule is applied (an ε-step); if a terminal, it's matched against the next input letter. A word is accepted exactly when the input is exhausted and the stack is empty.

step.title: CF grammar → pushdown automaton (lecture notes 7.12)
step.detail: A single state {{q}}; the stack starts with {{z0}}. First (q, ε, {{z0}}) → (q, {{start}}{{z1}}): the start variable goes onto the stack, {{z1}} below it. A variable on top: for every rule A → α, (q, ε, A) → (q, α) — {{ruleCount}} such steps. A terminal on top: (q, a, a) → (q, ε) matches it with the next input letter — {{terminalCount}} such steps. Finally (q, ε, {{z1}}) → (q, ε): when the sentential form is used up, the stack empties, and the word is accepted with an empty stack.

needsContextFree.title: ε-removal works on grammars of A → α rules
needsContextFree.detail: The procedure of lecture notes 6.3.1 leaves variables out of right-hand sides, so every left-hand side must be a single variable. The Chomsky classification panel shows which rule breaks this.

step1.title: 1. Nullable variables (lecture notes 6.3.1)
step1.detailNone: No nullable variable — the grammar is already ε-free.
step1.detailSome: N₁ holds the variables with an ε-rule; N(i+1) adds every A that has a rule A → α where every symbol of α is already in N(i). It stops when a round adds nothing. Nullable (derivable to ε): {{nullable}}.

step2.title: 2. Extending the rules
step2.detail: Every rule is replaced by all of its variants in which some of the nullable variables are dropped — except the empty right-hand side and the useless A → A. The ε-rules themselves are discarded.

step3.title: 3. New start variable because of ε
step3.detail: The original language contains ε (the start variable is nullable), so we introduce a new start variable {{s2}}: {{s2}} → {{start}} | ε. This way the ε-rule remains only on the start variable.

step1.title: 1. The graph of unit rules (lecture notes 6.3.2)
step1.detail: Unit rules (A → B): {{edges}}. U(A) is the set of variables reachable from A along them, A included.
step1.detailNone: There is no unit rule (A → B) — the grammar stays the same.

step2.title: 2. New rules
step2.detail: The unit rules are dropped, and every A gets the other rules B → β of each B ∈ U(A) as A → β.

epsilonFirst.title: The grammar still has ε-rules
epsilonFirst.detail: Removing the ε-rules afterwards can create new unit rules (A → BC with a nullable C gives A → B), so the lecture notes remove the ε-rules first.

step1.title: 1. Variables that derive a terminal word (lecture notes 6.3.3)
step1.detail: B₀ = Σ, and Bᵢ₊₁ adds every A with a rule A → α whose symbols are all in Bᵢ. The variables outside the final set derive no terminal word; their rules are dropped: {{removed}}.
step1.detailNone: B₀ = Σ, and Bᵢ₊₁ adds every A with a rule A → α whose symbols are all in Bᵢ. Every variable derives a terminal word.

step2.title: 2. Symbols reachable from the start variable
step2.detail: T₀ = {S}, and Tᵢ₊₁ adds every symbol on the right-hand side of a rule of a variable in Tᵢ. Unreachable, dropped: {{removed}}.
step2.detailNone: T₀ = {S}, and Tᵢ₊₁ adds every symbol on the right-hand side of a rule of a variable in Tᵢ. Every remaining symbol is reachable.

emptyLanguage.title: The language is empty
emptyLanguage.detail: The start variable {{start}} derives no terminal word, so L(G) = ∅ — every rule is useless.

needsEpsilonFree.title: The Chomsky normal form needs an ε-free grammar
needsEpsilonFree.detail: The construction assumes that ε occurs only as S → ε with S on no right-hand side; remove the ε-rules first.

epsilonDropped.title: ε is left out
epsilonDropped.detail: A grammar in Chomsky normal form cannot generate ε, so the rule {{start}} → ε is dropped: the result generates L(G) \ {ε}.

step2.title: Dropping the ε-rule (lecture notes 6.25)
step2.detail: The rule {{start}} → ε is dropped: there is no ε-rule in Chomsky normal form.

step3.title: Variables for the terminals
step3.detail: In every right-hand side of length at least 2, a terminal a is replaced by a new variable X_a with the rule X_a → a.

step4.title: Breaking the long rules
step4.detail: A → B₁B₂…Bₖ (k > 2) becomes A → B₁C₁, C₁ → B₂C₂, …, Cₖ₋₂ → Bₖ₋₁Bₖ with new variables Cᵢ.

already.title: Already in Chomsky normal form
already.detail: Every rule is A → a or A → BC.

needsCNF.title: CYK needs a grammar in Chomsky normal form
needsCNF.detail: Every rule must be A → a or A → BC.
